content: Acute sinusitis is a frequent condition that leads many individuals to seek primary medical care. It is characterized by significant symptoms such as facial pain, nasal congestion, headaches, thick nasal discharge, fever, and coughing. These symptoms often disrupt daily life, causing individuals to miss work or school. The treatment of sinusitis primarily aims to address the underlying causes and manage both the inflammatory and infectious aspects of the condition. The intranasal administration of a frozen, dried, natural fluid extract derived from the Cyclamen europaeum plant is believed to offer therapeutic benefits. This extract is thought to alleviate nasal congestion by promoting drainage of the sinuses and may also exert anti-inflammatory effects. The objective of this study was to evaluate the clinical effectiveness of topical intranasal Cyclamen europaeum extract in both adults and children diagnosed with acute sinusitis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in January 2018 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and clinical trial registries such as ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). Additional studies were identified by reviewing reference lists of included studies and contacting trial authors for further information. The inclusion criteria for the analysis were randomized controlled trials that compared intranasal Cyclamen europaeum extract to placebo, antibiotics, intranasal corticosteroids, or no treatment in individuals with acute sinusitis. The diagnosis of acute sinusitis was confirmed either through clinical evaluation supported by nasal endoscopy or radiological imaging. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the quality of the trials using standard Cochrane methodological procedures. Ultimately, two randomized controlled trials were included in the analysis. These trials involved a total of 147 adult outpatients with radiologically or endoscopically confirmed acute sinusitis. Participants were assigned to receive either Cyclamen europaeum nasal spray or a placebo for a treatment duration of up to 15 days. The risk of selection and detection bias in these studies was unclear, as neither trial reported details regarding allocation concealment or blinding of outcome assessors. Attrition rates were notably high in one of the studies, with 60% of participants dropping out; however, the dropout rates were balanced between the treatment and placebo groups. Neither of the included studies reported on the primary outcomes of interest, which were the proportion of participants whose symptoms resolved or improved at 14 days and 30 days. No serious adverse events or complications related to the treatment were observed. However, mild adverse events were more frequently reported in participants receiving Cyclamen europaeum compared to those receiving placebo. These adverse events included nasal and throat irritation, mild nosebleeds (epistaxis), and sneezing. Specifically, 50% of participants in the Cyclamen europaeum group experienced these mild side effects, compared to 24% in the placebo group (risk ratio 2.11, 95% confidence interval 1.35 to 3.29). The evidence supporting this finding was of moderate quality. In conclusion, the effectiveness of Cyclamen europaeum extract for the treatment of acute sinusitis remains uncertain. While no serious side effects were reported, a higher proportion of participants in the Cyclamen europaeum group experienced mild adverse events compared to those in the placebo group.
